newsitem.title: NORWAY: EU prepares to fine charterers of substandard ship.
newsitem.headline: EU prepares to fine charterers of substandard ship.

text.p: The European Commission is preparing laws to fine cargo owners who charter substandard ships, the EU head of maritime safety said on Wednesday.

Speaking at the Nor-Shipping 97 conference in Oslo, Roberto Salvarani, head of the EU maritime safety unit, said, "We are preparing new legislation which would place sanctions on charterers taking substandard ships.
"If a ship is detained for major deficiencies, financial sanctions would be applied to the cargo owner who has chartered the vessel."
Salvarani said the EU had agreed to run a three-month campaign concentrating on whether ships had complied with the International Safety Management code when it was introduced on July 1, 1998.

"Substandard ships will be detained in port until repairs are completed. If they do not comply they will be banned forever from European ports," he said. Two owners have already been banned for nine months for not complying with port state instructions, he added.

The Commission has also backed up International Association of Classification Societies action to suspend membership of the Polish register by removing its right to make statutory surveys of European-flagged ships, he said.
Salvarani said the action meant ships under the Polish register would have to flag outside the European Union. That would make them automatic targets for enhanced ship inspections.
He said the EU would review the Polish register once it had been re-admitted to the IACS.

The EU was also examining the Portuguese register over its links with French classification society Bureau Veritas. The EU wants to ensure that the relationship will enable the Portuguese society to implement all new regulations, he said.
He added that the EU is also auditing the Russian and Hellenic registers.
Salvarani stressed that self-regulation by the industry was the ultimate aim of all EU action. It did not want to add new laws if possible but would rather see existing regulations enforced.

However, the EU's role was to pressure owners into taking safety action, and he hoped the dry cargo sector could develop an industry-wide inspection system similar to that used by oil majors to vet tankers.
